paragraphs: Friend, here's what I want you to carry out of this one. The leaders at the gate thought the city made them safe. They had a slogan about being the meat in the pot, and God said the pot was never going to protect them (Ezekiel 11:3, 7). He knows what's in our minds before we say a word (Ezekiel 11:5). So the safe place isn't the one we feel sure about. It's the one where we actually follow Him.

Now look at who the people of Jerusalem wrote off. They said the exiles were "far away from the LORD," and God answered that He had been a "sanctuary" for them in the very countries He sent them to (Ezekiel 11:15, 16). Far from home is not far from God. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, and I can tell you that a dark place is not a God-forsaken place. Whatever you're in right now, He can be a sanctuary there too.

And then comes the part I love, the promise that is bigger than the problem. God says, "I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh," so they may follow His statutes (Ezekiel 11:19, 20). We can't squeeze a stone heart soft by ourselves, and I've tried with a lot of stubborn dough. God does the changing, and the following comes after. The glory leaves the city in this passage, and the story isn't over (Ezekiel 11:23). Ezekiel doesn't keep what he saw to himself, and neither should you.
